approaches.name: Extended iliofemoral approach to the acetabulum
approaches.corridor: Extensile lateral exposure created by posterior reflection of the abductors and short external rotators, with optional anterior extension into the iliac window

sources.title: Extended iliofemoral approach to the acetabulum
Extensile Extended Iliofemoral Approach to Acetabulum

procedure_applications.condition: A complex pattern cannot be reduced through a less-extensile posterior exposure
Combined lateral and anterior innominate-bone exposure is required

positioning.text: Position lateral on a radiolucent or fracture table with the entire buttock, hemipelvis, and limb accessible for manipulation and imaging.

setup.text: Prep from the posterior midline to the umbilicus and include the buttock and thigh while isolating the groin and perineum.

surface_landmarks.text: Mark the posterior and anterior superior iliac spines, iliac crest, greater trochanter, and lateral femoral shaft.

incision.text: Use an inverted-J incision from the posterior iliac region along the crest to the ASIS, then continue distally over the anterolateral thigh to permit posterior flap reflection.

superficial_interval.text: Develop the separately innervated abdominal-wall–gluteal interval along the iliac crest and the sartorius–tensor fasciae latae interval anteriorly.

deep_interval.text: Elevate the gluteal flap subperiosteally from the external ilium, then release gluteus minimus, gluteus medius, piriformis, and the conjoined short external rotators with repairable tendon stumps.

layers.text: Skin and large musculocutaneous flap, fascia lata and tensor interval, subperiosteal external-iliac exposure, abductor and short-external-rotator releases, then capsule and acetabular columns.

structures_encountered.text: The approach encounters lateral femoral circumflex branches, superior gluteal neurovascular pedicle, sciatic nerve, abductors, short external rotators, rectus origins, and hip capsule.

structures_at_risk.text: The superior gluteal artery, veins, and nerve are at high risk where they exit the greater sciatic notch and travel on the deep gluteal surface.
The sciatic nerve and medial femoral circumflex artery are at risk during short-external-rotator release, notch retraction, and posterior exposure.

danger_zones.text: Continuously assess gluteal-pedicle perfusion during posterior flap retraction; pedicle thrombosis can cause catastrophic flap necrosis.

retraction_hazards.text: Avoid aggressive or prolonged gluteal and sciatic-nerve retraction and protect neurovascular structures crossing the greater sciatic notch throughout reduction and fixation.

exposure.text: Exposes nearly the entire lateral innominate bone and posterior acetabulum, with anterior extension into the internal iliac fossa when required.

limitations.text: This highly morbid exposure demands complex flap mobilization and reconstruction and should be reserved for reductions not achievable safely through less-extensile approaches.

extensions.text: Extend anteriorly into the first ilioinguinal window for internal iliac-fossa access; a trochanteric osteotomy can preserve abductor insertions as a mobilized osseous fragment.

indications.text: A salvage extensile option for complex acetabular fracture patterns whose columns, dome, or chronic displacement cannot be reduced through standard anterior or posterior exposures.

relative_contraindications.text: Avoid when a less-extensile approach can achieve reduction or when soft-tissue condition, vascular disease, or inability to tolerate prolonged surgery makes the flap risk unacceptable.

implant_implications.text: The broad exposure allows multiplanar column fixation, but implants and retractors must not compromise the superior gluteal pedicle, sciatic nerve, or femoral-head blood supply.

fluoroscopy_implications.text: Use a radiolucent setup that preserves AP and Judet views despite lateral positioning and the large reflected flap.

closure.text: Perform anatomic, mechanically secure repair of capsule, short external rotators, gluteus medius and minimus, rectus origin, iliac-crest muscle origins, fascia, and superficial layers.

complications.text: Major complications include superior-gluteal hemorrhage or thrombosis, gluteal-flap necrosis, sciatic or superior-gluteal neuropathy, abductor failure, heterotopic ossification, infection, and wound breakdown.

bailouts.text: For uncontrolled superior-gluteal bleeding, pack the notch and obtain definitive vascular control or angiographic embolization; do not pursue blind clamping into the pelvis.

questions.question: Which vascular pedicle determines viability of the reflected gluteal flap?
questions.answer: The superior gluteal artery and accompanying veins.

questions.question: Why is aggressive gluteal-flap retraction dangerous?
questions.answer: It can obstruct or thrombose the superior gluteal pedicle, causing flap necrosis, and can injure the superior gluteal nerve.

approaches.name: Extensile lateral approach to the calcaneus
approaches.corridor: Full-thickness lateral calcaneal artery flap elevated strictly subperiosteally with the lateral ligaments and inferior peroneal retinaculum

procedure_applications.condition: Broad visualization of a displaced intra-articular or severe calcaneal fracture is required
Extensile lateral hindfoot access is selected

positioning.text: Position lateral or floppy lateral with the operative hindfoot uppermost and supported so the lateral calcaneus and fluoroscopic views remain accessible.

setup.text: Delay surgery until swelling has subsided and lateral skin wrinkles return; protect fracture blisters and confirm flap viability before incision.

surface_landmarks.text: Mark the Achilles tendon, lateral malleolus, base of the fifth metatarsal, junction of lateral and plantar skin, and posterior midline.

incision.text: Create a gently curved L-shaped incision with the vertical limb posterior to the lateral malleolus/Achilles border and the horizontal limb at the lateral–plantar skin junction toward the fifth-metatarsal base.

superficial_interval.text: Cut directly to bone at the corner and raise one full-thickness flap without undermining skin or separating the lateral calcaneal arterial supply.

deep_interval.text: Continue strictly subperiosteally, elevating periosteum, lateral collateral ligament, and inferior peroneal retinaculum together; split abductor digiti minimi in line with its fibers.

layers.text: Skin and full-thickness soft-tissue flap, subperiosteal lateral-wall plane with ligament/retinacular sleeve, lateral calcaneal wall, then subtalar posterior facet.

structures_encountered.text: The flap contains the lateral calcaneal arterial network, sural nerve, peroneal tendons and retinaculum, lateral ankle ligaments, abductor digiti minimi, and periosteum.

structures_at_risk.text: The lateral calcaneal artery and its anastomoses are the critical flap blood supply; leaving the subperiosteal plane or malpositioning either incision limb risks necrosis.
The sural nerve is at risk near the superior vertical limb and should be protected by correct posterior incision placement rather than aggressive isolation.

danger_zones.text: Do not place the vertical limb too anterior, the horizontal limb too superior, or dissect off the periosteum; each error jeopardizes flap perfusion and wound healing.

retraction_hazards.text: Use gentle periosteal sutures or carefully placed retractors; avoid fibular K-wire retraction that can injure the lateral calcaneal artery and increase wound breakdown.

exposure.text: Provides broad visualization of the lateral calcaneal wall, tuberosity, anterior process, calcaneocuboid region, and posterior subtalar facet.

limitations.text: The approach is invasive and soft-tissue dependent; it carries more wound risk than limited approaches and should not be used through swollen or compromised skin.

extensions.text: The distal subperiosteal interval can be developed toward the calcaneocuboid joint, while posterior-facet visualization can be increased between flexor hallucis longus and peroneal tendons.

indications.text: Used for ORIF of displaced intra-articular and severe calcaneal fractures and selected elective hindfoot reconstructions requiring broad lateral visualization.

relative_contraindications.text: Do not proceed with substantial swelling, absent wrinkle sign, threatened lateral skin, active infection, or patient factors that make flap healing unacceptably unreliable.

implant_implications.text: Keep plates and prominent hardware away from the flap apex and verify that fixation does not entrap peroneal tendons or penetrate the subtalar joint.

fluoroscopy_implications.text: Maintain access for lateral, axial heel, and Broden-type subtalar views to assess reduction, height, width, alignment, and joint penetration.

closure.text: Perform tension-free layered closure of deep fascia and abductor fascia followed by meticulous skin closure; use a drain selectively to limit hematoma.

complications.text: Key complications are flap-tip necrosis, wound dehiscence, deep infection, sural neuropathy, peroneal-tendon irritation, subtalar stiffness, and hardware prominence.

bailouts.text: If the flap appears ischemic or cannot close without tension, stop further insult, reassess fixation prominence, obtain soft-tissue expertise, and use staged or alternative management rather than forced closure.

questions.question: What clinical sign is commonly used to judge readiness for extensile lateral calcaneal surgery?
questions.answer: Return of lateral skin wrinkles—the wrinkle sign.

questions.question: Which artery is central to survival of the lateral calcaneal flap?
questions.answer: The lateral calcaneal artery, usually a terminal branch of the peroneal artery.

questions.question: What deep-dissection plane protects the flap blood supply?
questions.answer: A strictly subperiosteal plane with periosteum and retinacular/ligamentous tissue elevated as one flap.
